children.text:
> Its easy to see what works in hindsight

Yes! Hence my comment about world models being where (ex-)"AI luminaries" go to die. They had a great idea and pushed it, advancing their career, but as you point out this does not provide even them with a better perspective on where things are going. When it comes to the next big thing they have no better chance than a fresh grad student has.

But simulation (in this round, world models) is how you get the current thing to perform 1% better. So they work on that, and because of their reputation loads of money and resources pours into it because they chose it ... and then the solution comes from a different place entirely.

Except things are changing too, and world models like Google and Meta and Mistral and ... are pursuing appear to be getting bypassed by the current tech. It's starting to look a lot like the "internal world model" of a transformer that you've shown 1 million youtube movies is better than a separate world model, probably because the resources they pour into their general chatbot models are still an order of magnitude above what they can pour into their world models.

Its easy to see what works in hindsight, but in reality with this sort of research you have to find an approach that’s working and keep pushing it and see where it goes.

The results so far from genie have been stunning, and its not obvious to me that another approach is guaranteed to end up better for all use cases.

My point was that there is also the possibility of AI intelligence improving to the point that there isn't a difference anymore. That whatever beats the next set of benchmarks (which of course won't be the simulator or world model) is so smart it is both a better solution to the problem the world simulator poses and a better world simulator all in one and a better tool for creatives to build games or content.

This has already happened to other ML fields. For example, there's not much point anymore to ASR models (just feed audio into LLMs) and the space that TTS models occupy is fast disappearing. Oh and it's not just that Qwen 3.6 is a good ASR in addition to being good at coding mario. Doing things this way, not using an ASR model is fundamentally more expressive. A whole bunch of companies started up on ASR + TTS "towers" (lots of models, Pipecat style) as they're called, and they're dead companies walking. Their tech has been surpassed by just bog-standard generic LLMs in a way that they will never get the upper hand again.

A chain of models approach, a separate ASR, will never do this: "you said you agree but I can hear you're sarcastic, so I'll explain again". Also getting a conversational tower to switch languages when the user does that (or when it makes sense in a language course) is not quite impossible but very, very hard. And yet feeding audio directly into Qwen will almost magically solve these problems better than I will ever do it (lightly finetuned). It's fundamentally better in every way (except perhaps speed, of course. Although arguably such a tower needs an LLM too, it'll just have way less tokens)

This point has long been passed for image recognition. Feeding a photo or screenshot into a full LLM along with a request on what to do beats the crap out of any OCR, image recognition, ... model every time these days.

And now there's also hints of world models just being bypassed. Just giving a finetuned model the last 50 video frames (surprisingly, that fits in context, especially at reduced resolution), movement statistics, motor power, status, ... of a robot and asking what to do actually works (with heavy finetuning, but I think it'll start working without). Well ... AND then distilling that knowledge into a much smaller model because B200 racks are more than a bit to heavy for a logistics robot to carry around. But we'll get over that.

It depends if the goal is a more accurate simulation, or if the goal is a tool for creatives to build games or content.

If it's the latter, I don't see a 'hole'.

That's the thing about machine learning over time, and the big hole in the whole world model idea. Time and time again we make simulations and train models and we think that loop will work. It never does.

And why not? Because the first model that can actually learn to handle the simulation not only can do the simulation internally too, but it can do it better than out simulation.

It's where (ex-)"AI luminaries" go to die. It's a way to make glacial, slow progress in the correct direction while never actually getting anywhere.

So we get to a point and people keep making complicated simulations of one kind or another ... and then someone (some model) who's never used the simulation, and doesn't need it for model training gets by far the highest score on every benchmark and everyone agrees the simulation was kind of beside the point.

I think what we're talking about though here in reality is our perception of the model's output.

Our perception in realtime needs to be better than our ability to remember things from the past.

It matters whether humans can pass the test or not.

Humans also get details wrong when they do stuff like this. So right away, we learn this isn't a limitation of AI. If you want to say that getting that wrong is "proof they don't have a world model", that cuts both ways - it means humans do just fine despite not having one of those either.

But that also lends us insight into fixing the issue on merit! If humans also obviously lack a world model, how do we cope with this? Sometimes we use "live action" and reality forces consistency. Sometimes we use editors and QA. Sometimes it ends up on a website listing every little shot-to-shot inconsistency in every single TV show and movie ever made.

And now you have a few clear ideas on how to train the next generation of image models to do better! And you can probably dramatically improve your own prompting by providing reference images, using consistent descriptions, etc..

So, hardly irrelevant.

Must we, every time the limitations of AI are discussed, always imagine some simpleton human to defend it? It's trite and rarely adds anything to the conversation. The point is to judge the model on its merits. If this is a good world model, then it's a good world model. It doesn't matter whether or not a human can recollect every detail about a familiar neighborhood. It's irrelevant

does your model of models admit the possibility of partial models?

the average human cannot vividly recollect a walk through a familiar neighborhood, much less invoke a coherent fantasy of going on such a walk. do they contain a world model?

I'm by no means anti-anything but I think what the comments are getting at is that these "world models" do not have a world model. It's a fundamental qualitative gap that no amount of compute has been able to close, just mask by everything else getting better.

This doesn't show up as much where the verifiable reward is "code compiles and tests pass" but you can still absolutely see it in things like movies, prose, or slide decks. Even frontier models are pretty bad at keeping track of narrative threads even as the technical quality drastically improves.

This begs the question of whether the gap can be closed just with more compute (presumably yes, or at least errors can be minimized beyond human capacity to see them) and is that going to be worth it with current tech (possibly no).
